claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its initial single-phase solid-solution state.
The initial CoCrFeNiTi state is a homogeneous, coarse-grained solid solution with minimal secondary phases or precipitates.
The low hardness and strength are governed by an absence of internal microstructural obstacles to dislocation motion.
Dislocations glide easily in untreated CoCrFeNiTi because significant barriers are absent.
Easy dislocation glide causes the low intrinsic hardness and strength of untreated CoCrFeNiTi.
Controlled annealing can induce nanoscale precipitates or short-range ordered clusters in CoCrFeNiTi.
The annealing-induced precipitates or ordered clusters act as barriers or pinning points for dislocation glide.
Impeding dislocation motion with the induced nanoscale obstacles increases work hardening.
Annealing will increase the hardness of CoCrFeNiTi relative to its untreated state.
Annealing will increase the yield strength of CoCrFeNiTi relative to its untreated state.
The hardness and yield-strength increases will be statistically significant.
TEM, SEM, or XRD will reveal a uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates or ordering clusters after annealing.
The induced nanoscale obstacles can be produced without disrupting the alloy's overall single-phase state.
The proposed comparison is between an as-cast untreated state and an annealed state tested by identical tensile, compression, and hardness methods.
The hypothesis is bounded to room-temperature, quasi-static deformation of single-phase CoCrFeNiTi.
Different compositions, severe thermomechanical processing, or extreme temperatures and strain rates may activate alternative deformation mechanisms.
The magnitude of strengthening depends on annealing parameters and on precipitate size and distribution.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant hardness or yield-strength increase would falsify the proposed explanation.
Failure of annealing to produce the expected nanoscale obstacles would falsify the claim that the starting weakness arises from an absence of dislocation barriers.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as forged/processed in one field but as as-cast in the comparison and baseline, so the nominal control state is not consistently defined.

The intervention is intended to form precipitates, while the boundary requires a single-phase state and XRD is used to verify that secondary phases do not develop. Distinct precipitates normally imply an additional phase unless the intended mediator is limited specifically to short-range order or coherent compositional fluctuations.
